That's the strongest signal there is that a post is worth something, and it brings new people onto X. A like costs nothing. Sending something to a friend means you're putting your name on it.

The rest of the list tells a bit of a similar story like a reply is 5, a quote is 5, sharing by DM is 5, following the author is 4, a share is 2.1, a repost is 1, and a like is 0.7. Literally I didn’t know that repost does almost nothing.

The negatives are brutal btw a report is -234, a mute is -59, "not interested" is -53 and a block is -31.

A reply from someone you follow who follows you back gets a 15x boost. Conversations between real connections matter most (and not bots!)

Reposts don't reach strangers. A filter drops a repost for anyone who doesn't follow the reposter. A quote is a new post, so it can travel much further. Quote beats repost so you always have to add your own thoughts to a post.

item.title: @omarsar0：【待 AI 概括】Great paper from MIT and NVIDIA. I think this is an important step toward personalized, accessible RSI. The best recipe changes with every model and precision, so experts usually redesign it by hand. QDA hands that loop to an agent that builds and tests candidates over many rounds. They s…
item.description:
Great paper from MIT and NVIDIA.

I think this is an important step toward personalized, accessible RSI.

The best recipe changes with every model and precision, so experts usually redesign it by hand. QDA hands that loop to an agent that builds and tests candidates over many rounds.

They show that QDA beats the strongest public recipes by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 points at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search.

Evaluation speed is what makes this work. Scoring one quantized reasoning model normally takes tens of GPU-hours. QDA scores each candidate in minutes by measuring its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces the agent never sees. Promising candidates then get long generations to catch repetition loops.

A shared library of public PTQ methods lets the agent combine them without porting each codebase by hand.

On the 320B MoE GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, QDA recovered 98.3% of FP8 accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every checkpoint runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23388

Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/qda-closed-loop-llm-quantization-design-with-agents-2611.23388

item.description:
Whoa, great and even excessive Marin Mochi (535B-A23B) checkpoint drop (in a good way!)

Comes with great tech report btw with insights into why / how components were picked (for training stability and GPU throughput).

Short fact sheet:

1) Latent MoE with an extra RMSNorm on the latent that made latent MoE actually work (better)

2) Classic 3:1 sliding-window/global gated GQA, partial RoPE (local) and NoPE (global)

item.title: @convequity：分析称Lumentum与Coherent面临来自多方竞争激光器稀缺性或难持续
item.description:
Lumentum ($LITE) and Coherent ($COHR) have pricing power because lasers are scarce. In our view that scarcity may not last, because competition is coming from four sides.

First, shared lasers. With optical amplifiers, one laser can feed several channels, and designers can add amplification where it is needed instead of relying on one high-power laser. That could mean fewer lasers sold per unit of bandwidth, or less demand for the highest-power products. The second risk falls mainly on Lumentum, because ultra-high-power CW lasers are now its core business.

Second, new architectures for short links. MicroVCSEL designs spread bandwidth across many small, slower lasers. MicroLEDs go further and replace lasers altogether in suitable applications.

Third, LiDAR companies are bringing their laser and amplifier know-how into data centres. Aeva ($AEVA) announced an amplifier with reported output above 630 mW and a joint development agreement for a major hyperscaler's deployment. MicroVision ($MVIS) introduced an external laser module for co-packaged optics and says it is in talks with potential licensees and development partners.

Fourth, making standard 100 mW CW lasers is fairly commoditized know-how, and many companies are trying to scale up production, including Semtech ($SMTC), Sivers, Nokia ($NOK) and MACOM ($MTSI).

Total optical revenue at both incumbents could still grow as networks expand. The risk is that customers gain more ways to obtain the light they need, which would weaken the pricing power that comes from scarce lasers.

item.title: @convequity：AI集群构建商正重新设计光链路以减少稀缺激光器依赖并降低成本
item.description:
AI cluster builders are redesigning optical links so they need fewer scarce lasers. Feeding eight channels from one laser is one way to do that.

Silicon is good at carrying and modulating light but poor at emitting it. So today's 1.6 Tbit/s transceivers depend on indium phosphide (InP) lasers, and the highest-power ones are expensive, difficult to manufacture and in short supply. A customer that relies on them cannot deploy faster than those lasers become available.

That gives customers a strong reason to change the design. One route separates two jobs: a continuous-wave (CW) laser supplies steady light and a silicon-photonics modulator encodes the data, which widens the choice of laser suppliers. Other routes are lower-power lasers embedded in the system, and microLED links that replace lasers in suitable applications.

Another route is sharing one laser, using semiconductor optical amplifiers (SOAs), chips that use electrical power to boost light. Our own illustration, not a disclosed product: one CW seed laser is split into four branches, four SOAs boost the light, and each branch is split again to feed two channels. That gives eight 200 Gbit/s channels from one seed laser plus four SOAs instead of eight lasers.

An ideal eight-way split leaves each channel one-eighth of the power, a loss of roughly 9 dB. The SOAs make up that loss, so the power does not all have to come from one high-power laser.

This is not eight times cheaper. SOAs use electricity, add manufacturing and integration cost, and add some noise. Splitting also works only when every channel uses the same wavelength.

item.title: @convequity：分析认为激光雷达开发商的光子学平台与波长技术对数据中心光学连接应用具有潜在契合度
item.description:
LiDAR developers have spent years solving three problems that data-centre optics now face, and in our view $AEVA's photonics platform and wavelength expertise are among the closest fits for the optical-connectivity applications we are considering.

The three problems are powerful lasers, many lasers packed densely into one compact package, and receivers that recover faint returning light in a noisy environment.

As optics move into co-packaged and near-packaged designs, more channels must fit in a small package, and several can share one laser. Sharing one laser across several channels requires a strong source and often amplification, which is where Aeva's products fit.

Wavelength matters because each band needs a different light-emitting semiconductor (the gain material that generates and amplifies the light), plus matching optics and receivers. You can't just retune a laser for a new band, so Aeva's indium phosphide (InP) platform gives it an edge over LiDAR peers working in other bands.

We also rank Aeva highly on readiness because it has already launched the business and a customer project. In August 2026 it announced an optical-connectivity business and a joint development agreement with an unnamed optical-engine provider for a major hyperscaler's deployment. item.title: @convequity：分析称腾讯全年资本开支约为美国超大规模云厂商单季水平，中国AI采用多由初创企业主导
item.description:
A full year of Tencent's capital spending is about what one US hyperscaler spends in a quarter

Tencent reported third-quarter 2026 results on 18 Nov. Capital spending was RMB81.4 billion, 47% above what analysts expected. Free cash flow was minus RMB69.1 billion, largely because Tencent paid in advance for computing infrastructure.

Revenue rose 8% and missed estimates, and the shares closed down 0.85%. The coverage was about AI spending running ahead of forecasts.

I read the same number as small.

RMB81.4 billion is about $12 billion. Four quarters at that rate is just under $50 billion a year.

The figure for a large US hyperscaler, meaning one of the biggest American cloud companies, is $200 billion to $300 billion of capital spending a year. That is $50 billion to $75 billion a quarter. So a full year of Tencent's spending at this rate is about what one large US hyperscaler spends in a single quarter.

Chinese tech giants are spending slowly on AI compared with American ones. I take three things from that gap.

1) Being a national champion guarantees nothing. A new technology wave can leave an incumbent behind, and Tencent's size has not put it in front on AI.

2) In China, startups lead most AI adoption and usage. In the US, the tech giants and the startups lead it together.

3) China's tech market is more open to competition than most investors assume. In Europe, governments backstop incumbents in a regulated market. China still has a freer market, where a startup can get ahead of a company of Tencent's size.

For investors, the capital spending of Tencent, or of any Chinese tech giant, is a poor measure of Chinese AI progress. Most of China's AI adoption is happening at startups, outside the giants.

item.title: @convequity：分析认为人形机器人硬件面临瓶颈，美方未来可能对中国产机器人零部件实施进口限制
item.description:
Genesis AI's $500 million round shows hardware is the bottleneck for humanoids, and I expect the US to restrict Chinese humanoid parts next

Genesis AI announced a $500 million Series A on 17 Nov, led by Khosla Ventures, Premji Invest and Eclipse, per TechCrunch. The company develops its own model and designs and builds its own humanoid, called Eno.

CEO Zhou Xian told TechCrunch that "the model architecture contributes to maybe 10% of the final [result]" and named hardware as the key bottleneck. Genesis's dexterous hands last only a few weeks of regular work before they need to be replaced, per TechCrunch. Eno was not ready to demonstrate, so the demo ran on two off-the-shelf robotic arms.

In my view the US leads in the models and software that control a humanoid. It is well behind China on the physical robot, meaning the hands, the actuators (the motors that move the joints) and the sensors. Dexterous hands are where the US is furthest behind. The models and software are the more valuable part, but they are worth little without hardware that keeps working.

I expect the tech-unsophisticated China hawks now leading White House industrial policy to restrict the import or use of humanoid parts sourced from China. No such rule has been proposed yet, and I think it is a matter of time. The White House is reportedly moving toward an FCC bar on new Chinese optical transceivers in US data centers, and Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO on 11 Nov looks to me like a result of the same pressure.

A ban would be a mistake, for three reasons.

1) US humanoid companies would pay more and wait longer for hands, actuators and sensors, the parts where the US is weakest. They would build and test fewer robots.

2) US models and software would run on fewer robots, which slows the US AI industry.

3) Chinese humanoid makers would keep their full hardware supply.

Genesis has chosen a contractor to start mass manufacturing in the US next year. I think a US supply of hands and actuators that matches China's will take much longer than that.

Investors should watch for any White House or Congress move on Chinese humanoid components. A restriction would delay US humanoid companies and give Chinese humanoid makers an advantage. And it is going to further indicate one cohort the AI industrial policy is inelligent and deliberative enough or not.

item.title: @convequity：分析指出美国对东南亚数据中心算力芯片实施的新规可能短期内放缓中国开源模型发布
item.description:
Steve Eisman's AI price-war call is early, because Chinese open-model releases are about to slow

On 17 Nov Steve Eisman said Chinese open-weight models, which anyone can download and run, cost about $0.20 per million tokens and are taking share from Anthropic and OpenAI flagship models priced at $2 to $10. He expects a price war that neither lab has the balance sheet to fight.

His call needs Chinese labs to keep releasing better open models. I expect those releases to slow sharply.

US chip restrictions pushed Alibaba ($BABA), ByteDance and other Chinese firms to rent computing capacity overseas. About 75% of China's overseas AI compute is forecast to be in Southeast Asia by the end of 2026, per Institute for Progress estimates. My view is that most of Alibaba's training compute runs through that rented capacity.

On 16 Nov the US Commerce Department released a rule under which data centers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia need a US license for advanced AI chips, including Nvidia's. Facilities already serving large Chinese customers have 90 days to apply, per CNBC. I think Alibaba is being cut off from that capacity.

Hugging Face's release on 17 Nov shows how much the open-model community depends on Alibaba. It published an adapter, a small add-on trained on top of an existing model, that lifted the pass rate on 51 hard coding tasks from 29% to 63%, per its model card. The adapter works only on Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B. A new base model needs a large training run, and the rule restricts the compute for those runs.

DeepSeek chose the harder route of integrating its models with Huawei's Ascend chips. I expect a strong DeepSeek model after the middle of 2027, and open-model competition picks up again then.

The timing makes me suspicious. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on 11 Nov, and the license rule came five days later. I read both as moves against open-source AI, and both help Anthropic around its IPO. I suspect whether Anthropic's stakeholders or their allies were involved.

For the next two quarters, enterprises and AI startups will have fewer good new open models to choose from. Some will spend a little more on closed models, and I think Anthropic gains most.

item.title: @convequity：分析认为企业级AI生产力应用普及速度可能慢于预期，验证和数据稀缺仍是主要挑战
item.description:
Enterprise productivity is AI's next growth curve, and it will arrive slower than Microsoft's Ignite pitch suggests

At Ignite on 17 Nov, Satya Nadella called Copilot the new operating system for work. I agree with the direction. Enterprise productivity is the next big market for AI after coding agents. I also think adoption will be slower, and the products weaker, than people expect.

Coding agents worked first for three reasons. A huge amount of code is public, so the models had training data. Code can be run and tested, so every output can be verified. And everything is code or an API, so a model can work in the environment with little integration.

Enterprise work is different on all three. The tasks are open-ended, the training data is scarce, and the results are hard to check. Nadella told Gergely Orosz the day before Ignite: "in a world where code generation has become cheap, what has become hard is verification." Verification is harder still for office work, where there is no test to run. Microsoft's new Agent 365 dashboard shows it.

Microsoft has one real strength here. It holds a lot of enterprise work data internally, and that data is what the models lack.

Microsoft also has one real weakness. It does not have a strong coding model or coding agent of its own. I think a strong coding agent is the base that an enterprise productivity agent should be post-trained from.

So the winner is still open. It could be Gemini, because Google can integrate it natively into its own apps. It could also be Grok from SpaceX. Grok's adoption is growing well, the team is working on this use case, and Grok is more vendor-neutral.

I would not assume Microsoft wins enterprise productivity because it owns the office suite.

item.title: @convequity：Anthropic发布仅限直接订阅和控制台使用的Code Mode，分析称将影响云服务商渠道收入占比
item.description:
Anthropic has released Code Mode, a new way for Claude to carry out agent tasks. It works only through Claude Code on a Claude subscription or an Anthropic Console account. Anthropic's docs rule out Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud and $MSFT's Foundry.

Code Mode changes how Claude uses tools, and the model still runs on Anthropic's servers. Normally Claude makes each tool call as a separate model turn. With Code Mode, Claude writes one script that runs in the user's terminal, calls the tools and returns only the output Claude needs.

Technically this is evolutionary. Anthropic has published no savings figure for Code Mode. Its closest number comes from the same technique on its API a year ago: 37% fewer tokens on complex research tasks. One early independent test of Code Mode, a single run, also measured 37% fewer input tokens, but with the same number of model requests and a slower finish. So Code Mode cuts tokens by about a third on tool-heavy tasks. The saving comes from Claude reading less tool output each step, not from fewer steps, so the dollar saving is likely smaller. That is useful and well short of a step change.

The channel matters more than the technology. About 44% of Anthropic's revenue in the first nine months of 2026 came through Amazon, Google and Microsoft cloud accounts, per the prospectus. Those customers cannot use Code Mode. An enterprise that wants it has to buy Claude directly, and Anthropic keeps more margin on every workload that moves.

Amazon and Google sit on both sides. As channels, they lose the middleman cut on each workload that goes direct. As holders of nearly 29% of Anthropic between them, they get part of it back through a more profitable Anthropic.

I will watch two things: whether Code Mode reaches Bedrock or Google Cloud, and the cloud-account share of revenue against today's 44%.

item.title: @omarsar0：麻省理工CSAIL等机构研究显示具备基础工具的冻结大模型无需显式引导即可自主实现自我改进
item.description:
Do LLM agents still need to be told how to self-improve?

A new paper from MIT CSAIL and the University of Tübingen tests this directly.

They give a frozen model a compute budget and simple tools. It can write practice games, watch another copy of itself play them, and edit that copy's prompt and skill files. It does not see real tasks or validation scores, and it is not told how to learn.

Capable models built a working learning procedure on their own and improved on held-out games with hidden mechanics.

Models from different families arrived at similar strategies. They wrote games at a calibrated difficulty, ran controlled A/B comparisons, built their own validation suites, and spent more effort on harder tasks. The text files they produced also improved play on external benchmarks with different horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.

This matters for safety as well. Leaving out an explicit self-improvement loop does not stop a capable model from improving itself when it has the tools.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23219

item.description:
How does a truly "AI-pilled" startup work? @harjotsgill spent $250K last month on AI agents, shipped 5,000 PRs and explains why this all makes sense - at least for CodeRabbit.

Timestamps:

1:21:55 Skills for the AI era

Brought to you by:

• @turbopuffer – a ridiculously scalable, fast and cheap hybrid search engine, built on top of object storage, used by cutting-edge companies like Anthropic, Linear, Ramp and others. https://turbopuffer.com/pragmatic

• @GoEntire – Entire launched its own Git forge, shipped Continuous Memory, and reinvented the pull request (called Trails). Trails are a much more natural workflow when agents keep pushing new changes. https://entire.io/pragmatic

• @WorkOS – WorkOS built Airlock, the authorization layer for AI agents. It evaluates every request against the agent’s intent + your rules, and either allows it, denies it, or routes it to a human. http://workos.com/airlock

Three interesting learnings:

1. For dev tooling startups like CodeRabbit, massive AI spend can be justified by launching new, AI-related products faster

It feels to me that CodeRabbit is not a typical company: its AI spending is a form of R&D if it creates new solutions that can be commercialized and sold. It’s not the same at places with fixed customer bases willing to pay a certain amount for an existing product, and no more.

Also, Harjot says that they got quoted $13M/year for a CI solution to handle their PR output, but the price made him decide they’d build their own CI system using agents. It took a week, and the new CI cost 50% less than the quote, with similar performance.

2. Human code review is dead, long live the human review!

Harjot thinks that we will stop reviewing code generated by agents. Instead, we’ll spend more time reviewing the planning and final asset. Inside of CodeRabbit, engineers are reviewing releases (multiple PRs), not individual PRs.

3. What Harjot looks for when hiring engineers: agency, breadth of experience, and systems thinking.

He posted an unconventional job ad, only inviting candidates who had shipped 1,000+, non-slop PRs in the past 30 days, or had played 500+ hours of strategy and management games like Civilization, Age of Empires, Transport Tycoon, or Factorio. Harjot says he cannot unsee the similarities between running dozens of agents in parallel and playing a strategy video game involving tracking what dozens of units do.

item.title: @convequity：美国联邦法院拒绝驳回DRAM反垄断集体诉讼，多方内存采购长期合约将进入原告证据发现程序
item.description:
The DRAM price-fixing case will put the HBM supply contracts in front of plaintiffs

A California federal judge has refused to dismiss a class action against Samsung, SK hynix and $MU. The suit says the three coordinated cuts to DDR4 output while moving capacity to HBM, the high-bandwidth memory used in AI chips. They control over 90% of DRAM, and the suit says prices rose more than 700% in a year and a half.

The ruling only lets the case go ahead. The companies say each one made its own decision in response to AI memory demand. Their answers are due 7 Dec, and a case-management conference is set for 12 Jan 2027.

We think the market is missing what comes next. Memory bulls point to Nvidia's multi-year memory purchase commitments as proof the shortage is structural. Those supply contracts are the documents plaintiffs will ask for in discovery, because they show when each maker decided to move wafers from DDR4 to HBM, and on what terms.

Two outcomes follow.

1) The three makers' DDR4 cuts line up closely in time. The contracts bulls cite then become evidence for the plaintiffs.

2) The timing differs by maker. The case then comes down to three companies each following demand, which is the companies' defense.

The next real event is discovery after the 7 Dec answers. A fine is not the near-term risk.

Micron is the liquid US listing, so MU will move most on each headline. Samsung and SK hynix carry the same exposure and would share any remedy.

Buyers carry risk too. Apple's long-term DRAM deal with Samsung reportedly fixes volume and leaves price open, so hardware makers outside memory take the price risk into 2027.
